szoveg_eredeti:
Fluent Dependence Framework Explains How Artificial Intelligence Masks Developing Human Capability

A newly published theoretical analysis in educational measurement and cognitive psychology indicates that delegating intellectual labor to artificial intelligence systems can systematically disconnect visible task execution from authentic human capability. In a comprehensive framework published in Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans, researchers Jeffrey Anderson and Sam Zaza synthesize four decades of cognitive load theory and contemporary empirical findings to formalize a construct they designate as fluent dependence. The researchers describe fluent dependence as a distinct capability state in which an individual successfully generates complex work product that satisfies evaluative standards through machine mediation while failing to construct the underlying cognitive schemas that the output appears to demonstrate. Unlike established concerns surrounding academic integrity, the authors demonstrate that this decoupling does not constitute cheating or deliberate rule evasion, but rather represents a fundamental measurement validity dilemma stemming directly from the architecture of human memory and machine assistance.

To illustrate the operational mechanism of this phenomenon, the authors point to an increasingly recognizable educational and organizational paradox. A student or early-career professional tasked with strategic analysis can utilize a generative model to produce sophisticated segmentation reasoning, coherent contextual recommendations, and rigorous framework applications that seamlessly satisfy grading rubrics or corporate quality benchmarks. Anderson and Zaza note that while the generated artifact was genuinely produced, the individual capability it ostensibly demonstrated was entirely illusory. The cognitive engagement required to solve the problem was executed by the artificial agent rather than internalized by the learner, creating a performance gap that remains functionally invisible until the mediating technology is structurally removed from the operating environment.

The theoretical framework grounds this divergence in cognitive load theory, first pioneered by John Sweller and elaborated across recent learning research. Human working memory possesses severe capacity limitations, typically restricted to managing between three and four distinct novel elements simultaneously, whereas long-term memory maintains an effectively unlimited store of complex structures known as schemas. Meaningful learning occurs when working memory processes intrinsic cognitive load—the inherent complexity of novel conceptual material—converting those challenging interactions into organized schemas within long-term memory through germane cognitive processing. When an artificial intelligence agent executes the analytical synthesis, relational organization, and structural integration on behalf of the user, the intrinsic load is transferred away from the biological brain to the external system. Consequently, while polished output is successfully generated, the germane processing required for schema construction fails to occur, leaving the human user without durable, independently retrievable competence.

This architectural explanation clarifies a body of empirical evidence that has emerged across multiple independent educational investigations. Students provided with unrestricted artificial intelligence access performed noticeably better on initial practice exercises but suffered an approximate seventeen percent reduction in examination grades once access was completely withdrawn, scoring worse than control peers who had never utilized the machine tutor. Similarly, university investigations conducted by Michael Stadler and colleagues observed that students utilizing large language models for scientific inquiry reported significantly lower perceived mental workload compared to peers conducting standard search engine queries, yet systematically produced demonstrably weaker conceptual reasoning. Rather than fostering mastery, unconstrained computational support reliably attenuated the effortful cognitive friction essential for conceptual development.

Anderson and Zaza explicitly delineate fluent dependence from existing psychological and human factors concepts to eliminate cross-disciplinary confusion. Academic cheating is fundamentally defined by subjective intent and procedural rule violation, whereas fluent dependence frequently occurs when individuals operate entirely in good faith, transparently disclose machine usage, and comply with all institutional guidelines. Similarly, while classical cognitive offloading—such as using printed calendars for scheduling or electronic calculators for arithmetic—is generally adaptive for bounded tasks whose sub-processes need not be internalized, artificial intelligence offloading targets open-ended analytical reasoning that learners must internalize to achieve professional autonomy. Furthermore, the construct diverges from automation complacency, which human factors researchers traditionally associate with monitoring lapses and vigilance failures in fixed industrial systems; fluent dependence instead targets the insidious erosion of developmental schema construction under fluid, conversational cognitive collaboration.

The framework also contextualizes fluent dependence against recent adjacent constructs including cognitive debt, algorithm overdependence, and metacognitive decoupling. Algorithm overdependence examines consumer reliance on recommendation algorithms that diminish autonomous market scrutiny. Most critically, metacognitive decoupling, described by Maria Fernandes and colleagues, captures the psychological distortion wherein technology users report elevated personal confidence and subjective mastery despite exhibiting diminished objective competence. Anderson and Zaza position metacognitive decoupling as a compounding amplifier of fluent dependence: because the artificial system effortlessly generates high-caliber outputs, users fall prey to an amplified illusion of competence, mistaking the fluent fluency of the generative software for their own developing intellectual capability.

From an educational measurement perspective, the paper frames fluent dependence as a construct validity crisis under the classical doctrines of Samuel Messick. Validity does not reside statically within a test or rubric, but within the defensibility of the inferences educators and institutions draw from observed performance. When an individual submits work developed through generative assistance, the artifact reflects joint human-machine performance rather than unassisted human capability. Assessing this composite product introduces severe construct-irrelevant variance, contaminating the inference of student mastery with external machine processing. Conversely, when institutions reactively revert to simplistic, artificial-intelligence-resistant assessment formats, they risk construct underrepresentation by failing to evaluate high-level integrative competencies. When credentialing bodies and academic institutions award certifications based upon joint-system outputs, their evaluations become systematically miscalibrated, certifying individuals for competencies that evaporate the moment computational support becomes unavailable or inappropriate.

To resolve this diagnostic challenge, Anderson and Zaza propose paired-task assessment as a rigorous empirical detection methodology. Because fluent dependence is an inherently relational gap construct, it cannot be identified through single-point performance evaluations. A well-designed paired-task assessment couples an artificial-intelligence-mediated assignment with an unmediated assignment targeting the exact same underlying competency at equivalent cognitive complexity and element interactivity.
